items.body: Home Guides Backing types: cut to shape, rectangle or stand Choosing your sign Backing types: cut to shape, rectangle or stand The tube gets all the attention, but the acrylic behind it decides how the sign sits in the room: barely there, a neat panel, or a freestanding piece. Here are the three backings and the five finishes, with your design drawn on each. 3 min read Updated 10 Oct 2026 By the Lit Neon workshop Copy link Choosing your sign On this page On this page Three backings Every sign is mounted on acrylic. You choose its shape in the designer, and the stage draws exactly what you’ve chosen. Cut to shape follows the outline of your letters with a small margin. On the wall it almost disappears, so the sign looks like light drawn straight onto the paint. It is the default, and the one most people pick for homes. Rectangle mounts the sign on a clean panel held off the wall on standoffs. It looks deliberate and graphic, keeps fiddly script tidy, and is easier to hang level. Table stand builds a foot into the acrylic so the sign stands on its own on a shelf, counter or bar. No holes in the wall at all. Try it Switch backing and finish on a rendered wall. The price difference is shown at Medium. Five finishes The acrylic can be clear, black, white, gold mirror or silver mirror. Clear is included and suits almost everything. The others change the character of the sign: Black makes the sign pop on a pale wall and hides the cable route. Very good on a rectangle in a bar. White looks crisp and gallery-like on a white or pastel wall, and softens the off-state. Gold or silver mirror doubles the glow and catches the room. They are glamorous on a wedding backdrop or a salon wall, and they look striking even when the sign is off. Coloured finishes cost a little more than clear. The designer shows the difference next to each one, and the demo above shows it at Medium. How each one looks switched off A sign spends a lot of its life switched off, so it is worth thinking about the daytime look. Cut to shape on clear acrylic is the most discreet: by day you see the white or tinted tube and very little else. A rectangle reads as a deliberate panel, more like a framed print, and a black or white rectangle looks finished even with the light off. Done well, it tells passers-by you’re open, gives your counter a focal point and turns up in your customers’ photos. items.title: Looking after your sign
items.excerpt: A soft cloth, the right spot and a dimmer used kindly. How to keep your sign glowing, plus what it really costs to run.
items.tags: Fitting and care · clean · care · dust · running cost · electricity · cost
items.body: Home Guides Looking after your sign Fitting and care Looking after your sign An LED neon sign asks very little of you. A dust now and then, a sensible spot on the wall and a bit of thought about the cable will keep it glowing for years. Here is the whole routine. 3 min read Updated 10 Oct 2026 By the Lit Neon workshop Copy link Fitting and care On this page On this page Cleaning, the five-minute version Switch it off and unplug it at the socket. Let it sit for a few minutes. Dust the tube with a dry, soft microfibre cloth or a soft make-up brush. Go along the tube, not across it. Wipe the acrylic with a barely damp microfibre cloth, then dry it. Acrylic scratches more easily than glass, so press lightly. Plug it back in once everything is completely dry. That’s it. Every few weeks in a dusty room, every couple of months in most homes. Never use glass cleaner Ammonia, alcohol-based sprays and solvents can cloud acrylic and dull the silicone jacket. Water and a soft cloth are all it needs. Where it’s happiest Indoors and dry. Our standard signs are made for indoor use. Bathrooms, steamy kitchens right above a hob and anywhere it could get splashed are best avoided. Out of strong sun. Years of direct sunlight through a window can fade a coloured jacket and age the acrylic. A spot out of the brightest light keeps it looking new. With room to breathe. The power supply likes a little air around it. Behind a sideboard is fine; buried under a pile of cushions isn’t. Cable without strain. Run the cable so it isn’t pulled tight or pinched by furniture, and don’t cut or shorten it. Using the dimmer kindly Add the dimmer and remote in the designer and you can dim your sign. Dimming is good for the mood and good for the sign: LEDs run cooler and use less power at lower brightness. Most people find their sign looks best a notch or two below full in the evening, and full brightness only when the room is busy. If the remote stops responding, try a fresh battery first and point it at the dimmer rather than the sign, since that is where the receiver lives. What it costs to run LED neon uses very little electricity, but “very little” isn’t a number. items.body: Home Guides Choosing colours: white jacket or coloured? Choosing your sign Choosing colours: white jacket or coloured? Every sign has two looks: lit at night, and switched off in daylight. Most people only think about the first. The jacket decides the second, and it is the choice people most often wish they had known about. 3 min read Updated 10 Oct 2026 By the Lit Neon workshop Copy link Choosing your sign On this page On this page What the jacket is LED neon is a strip of LEDs inside a silicone tube. That silicone sleeve is the jacket. It diffuses the light into a smooth line, and it decides what the sign looks like when it’s off. A white jacket looks white, a little like frosted glass, when the sign is off. Switch it on and it glows your colour. It is the classic look, and it means the sign reads as a neat white drawing on the wall by day. A coloured jacket is tinted to match the light. It keeps its colour by day, so a pink sign looks pink even when it’s off, and lit it can look a touch richer. Neither is better. A white jacket is calmer in a light room and lets one sign suit any decor by day. A coloured jacket makes a statement around the clock, which is lovely in a bar, a nursery or a bold wall. Rendered previews, not photographs. Choosing the colour itself A few things we’ve learned from drawing a lot of signs: Warm white is the most forgiving. It suits bedrooms, living rooms and weddings, and it photographs beautifully. If you can’t decide, start here. Pinks and reds read as neon. If you want the sign to say “neon” loudly, hot pink or red does it. Blues and greens are cooler and calmer. Ice blue is lovely in a modern room; electric blue and green are punchy in a games room or a bar. Think about the wall. A sign glows onto the wall behind it. items.body: Home Guides How LED neon is made How it’s made How LED neon is made Every sign starts as a drawing you approve and ends as a box on your doorstep. In between, your words go through five stages. Here is what happens at each one, and why we do it in that order. 4 min read Updated 10 Oct 2026 By the Lit Neon workshop Copy link How it’s made On this page On this page Five stages, one drawing An LED neon sign is simple to describe and fiddly to make well. It is a flexible strip of LEDs inside a silicone tube, shaped into letters and fixed to a sheet of clear acrylic, with a cable running to a power supply and a dimmer. The skill is in the shaping: how smoothly the tube follows a curve, how cleanly the letters join, how evenly it glows. The illustrated strip below follows your own words through the five stages. It is a drawing of the process, not footage of our bench, and it uses whatever you last typed into the designer. Illustrated How your sign is made, drawn with your words. 1. Drawn: the proof you approve When you order, a designer turns your design into a production drawing: the exact words and lettering, each line’s colour, the overall width and height, and the outline of the acrylic backing. We send you that drawing within 12 hours, and nothing is made until you approve it. This step matters more than any other. A neon sign is made to your words, so the drawing is the contract between us. Check the spelling, the line breaks and the size; tweaks at this stage are free. Once you approve, the sign is made exactly as drawn. 2. Shaped: tube along the lines The LED tube is shaped along the centre line of each letter, following the drawing. Script lettering is the trickiest, because the tube has to flow through loops and joins without kinks, while block lettering needs crisp corners. Where a letter can’t be drawn in a single run of tube, it is split into sections that meet invisibly, and the LEDs are positioned so the glow stays even across the join. This is also why some very fine lettering has a minimum size. Below a certain letter height a tube simply can’t follow a tight curve, so the designer only offers sizes each lettering can actually be made at. 3. Mounted: the acrylic backing The shaped tube is fixed to a sheet of clear acrylic. You choose the backing in the designer: cut to the outline of your letters, a rectangle panel, or a table stand. items.body: Home Guides How to hang a neon sign Fitting and care How to hang a neon sign Hanging a neon sign is closer to hanging a mirror than wiring a light. It plugs into a normal socket, so the only decision is how it meets the wall. There are four ways, and one of them will suit your wall. 3 min read Updated 10 Oct 2026 By the Lit Neon workshop Copy link Fitting and care On this page On this page First, choose the method You pick the hanging method in the designer, and the kit comes to match. The right one depends on your wall, the size of the sign and whether you can drill. Wall screws and standoffs are the classic. The sign sits a little way off the wall on four small posts, which looks tidy and lets the glow wash the wall behind. Best for plaster or brick and for any sign you want to stay put. Hanging chains hang the sign from two hooks or a picture rail. Good when you’d rather make two holes than four, or when you want to move the sign about. Adhesive strips mean no drilling at all. They are for small, light signs on smooth, sound walls, which makes them handy for renters. A table stand turns the sign into a freestanding piece for a shelf, a sideboard or a bar. It is chosen as a backing in the designer, because the stand is part of the acrylic. Not sure? The demo below has a two-question helper that recommends a method and explains why, and it shows your sign mounted each way with the steps drawn out. Try it Four ways to hang, shown with your sign. The steps are an illustration. Before you start Find the socket. Hold the sign where you want it and check the cable reaches a socket without stretching. Plan where the power supply and the dimmer will sit, usually behind furniture. Check the wall. Use a detector to make sure there are no pipes or cables where you’ll drill. Above a socket or a light switch, cables often run straight up or down. Mark the position with masking tape. Stand back, look at it from where you’ll usually see it, and adjust before you make a single hole. Wall screws and standoffs, step by step Hold the sign against the tape and mark through each of the pre-drilled holes in the acrylic with a pencil. Drill at the marks, using the right bit for your wall, and push in the wall plugs. Screw the back half of each standoff into the wall. items.body: Home Guides LED neon vs glass neon: what you’re actually buying How it’s made LED neon vs glass neon: what you’re actually buying Say “neon sign” and most people picture glass: hand-bent tubes humming above a diner. What most people buy today is LED neon. They look similar from across a room and very different up close. Here is the honest comparison. 3 min read Updated 10 Oct 2026 By the Lit Neon workshop Copy link How it’s made On this page On this page What glass neon is Traditional neon is glass tubing heated and bent by hand, then filled with a small amount of gas and sealed. A high voltage across the gas makes it glow. Neon gas itself glows red-orange; other colours come from different gases and from coatings on the inside of the glass. It is a genuine craft, practised by a shrinking number of glass benders, and a well-made glass sign has a depth of light that is hard to match. What LED neon is LED neon is a strip of small LEDs inside a flexible silicone tube. The silicone diffuses the light, so instead of a row of dots you see a continuous line, which is what gives it the neon look. The tube is shaped into letters and fixed to an acrylic backing, and it runs from a low-voltage power supply that plugs into an ordinary socket. The colour comes from the LEDs and from the silicone jacket around them. A white jacket looks white when the sign is off and glows your colour when it’s on; a coloured jacket keeps its colour by day as well. Our guide to choosing colours goes into that properly. items.body: Home Guides How big should your neon sign be? Choosing your sign How big should your neon sign be? The most common regret with a neon sign isn’t the colour or the lettering. It’s buying it a size too small. Here is how to get it right first time, using the wall you actually have. 4 min read Updated 10 Oct 2026 By the Lit Neon workshop Copy link Choosing your sign On this page On this page Size starts with letter height We size signs by the height of the letters, not by the overall width. That sounds backwards until you notice that the same letter height gives you a short sign for “Hi” and a long one for “Happily ever after”. Letter height decides how bold the sign feels and how far away it reads; the number of letters decides how wide it ends up. There are five sizes in the designer, from Small to Statement. The table below shows each letter height and how wide one familiar phrase comes out at every size, measured in the same lettering the designer uses. Your own words will be wider or narrower depending on how many letters they have and which lettering you pick. Anything wider than 2 m we quote by hand, because big signs need a closer look at how they’re fixed and powered. The designer tells you the moment your words cross that line and suggests a size that fits. Let the furniture decide A sign rarely hangs on an empty wall. It goes above a bed, a sofa, a sideboard or a bar, and that piece of furniture is the best ruler you own. A sign that is roughly half to three-quarters the width of the furniture underneath looks deliberate. Smaller than half and it starts to float; wider than the furniture and it competes with it. Above a double bed: 80 to 100 cm wide reads well, centred on the headboard. Above a three-seat sofa: 100 to 140 cm, with the bottom of the sign a hand’s width or two above the sofa back. items.body: Home Guides My sign won’t light: a calm checklist Fitting and care My sign won’t light: a calm checklist Nine times out of ten, a sign that won’t light is a plug that isn’t quite in, or a remote that has turned it right down. Work along the chain from the wall to the sign and you will usually find it in under five minutes. 3 min read Updated 10 Oct 2026 By the Lit Neon workshop Copy link Fitting and care On this page On this page How a sign is connected Power travels in one line: from the wall socket, through the power supply, into the dimmer, and from the dimmer to the sign. If any link in that chain is loose or switched off, the sign stays dark. So the trick is to check the links in order, starting at the wall. Illustrated The parts in your box and how they connect. Tap a number to see what each part does. The checklist Go through it one step at a time. Tap “That fixed it” the moment the sign lights, or “Yes, done” to move to the next check. Is the socket on? Check the switch on the wall socket, then plug a lamp or a phone charger into the same socket to prove it works. Extension leads and smart plugs have their own switches too. Is the power supply plugged in all the way? Push the UK plug firmly into the socket. If the power supply has a small indicator light, it should be lit. No light usually means no power reaching it. Is the supply connected to the dimmer? The cable from the power supply plugs into the dimmer. These connectors can look pushed in when they’re only half home. Unplug it, look inside for anything bent, then push it in firmly until it stops. Is the dimmer connected to the sign? Do the same with the connection between the dimmer and the sign’s own cable. If the connector screws or clips together, make sure it’s fully tightened. Has the remote turned it off or right down? Press the on button on the remote, then hold brightness up for a few seconds. Point it at the dimmer, not the sign, since that’s where the receiver is. Try a fresh battery if nothing happens. Does it light without the dimmer? If your dimmer can be bypassed, connect the power supply straight to the sign for a moment. If the sign lights, the dimmer is the problem, and that is covered by your warranty. items.body: Home Legal Recycling your sign Legal Recycling your sign A sign should last for years, but nothing lasts for ever. When it’s time, the LEDs, the power supply and the remote’s battery all deserve better than the bin. Last updated 10 Oct 2026 Draft for the owner: not yet reviewed by a lawyer On this page On this page What the crossed-out bin means Our signs, power supplies and dimmers carry the crossed-out wheelie bin. It means they’re electrical equipment that mustn’t go in your household rubbish. They contain materials that can be recovered and some that shouldn’t end up in landfill, so they need to go to a proper electrical recycling point. Send an old sign back to us When you buy a new sign from us, we’ll take back an old one of the same kind, whoever made it, so it can be recycled properly. Get in touch through our contact form with your order reference and we’ll explain how to send it. You can also drop electrical items at most household waste and recycling centres run by your council, free of charge. Your council’s website lists the nearest one. Taking it apart sensibly The sign and its tube: treat the whole sign as electrical waste. Please don’t try to separate the LED tube from the acrylic. The power supply and dimmer: electrical waste, same as the sign. The remote’s battery: take it out and recycle it at a battery collection point; most supermarkets have one by the door. The box and paper packaging: your household recycling. Our producer registration We meet our obligations as a seller of electrical equipment under the UK’s Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment
